konular: Prefill vs. decode and KV cache

sorular.soru: What is the main rationale for using pre-RMSNorm (y = x + F(RMSNorm(x))) instead of post-LayerNorm (y = LN(x + F(x)))?
secenekler: Because normalization is applied after the residual addition, the output scale of each block is fixed.
Because the residual path carries x forward directly, gradient flow is easier in deep stacks.
Because RMSNorm has no β parameter, the number of learned parameters per block is reduced.
Because attention and the FFN share a single normalization layer, the computational cost is lower.
sorular.aciklama: In pre-norm, the residual path carries x forward without passing through any normalization; this is why gradient flow is easier in deep Transformer stacks. The first option is the definition of post-LayerNorm; the absence of β is a difference between RMSNorm and LayerNorm and has nothing to do with pre/post placement of the norm.

sorular.soru: The vector h = [1, 3, 5, 7] is fed into an RMSNorm layer, and γ = 1 is assumed. By the RMSNorm definition, approximately what value are the components of h divided by?
sorular.aciklama: RMS(h) = √mean(h²) = √((1+9+25+49)/4) = √21 ≈ 4.58. 2.24 (√5) is the standard deviation of the mean-subtracted components, which would be LayerNorm's divisor, whereas RMSNorm does not subtract the mean. 9.17 (√84) results from forgetting to divide the sum of squares by 4, and 4.00 is the arithmetic mean of the components.

sorular.soru: In the expression SwiGLU(x) = (SiLU(xW_gate) ⊙ xW_up)W_down, what is the function of the SiLU(xW_gate) path?
secenekler: Clipping negative intermediate activations to zero to produce a sparse intermediate representation like ReLU
Mixing information across tokens to complete the work of the attention sublayer
Scaling the channels produced by xW_up element-wise with a learned gate
Normalizing the scale of the intermediate representation with RMS before the W_down projection
sorular.aciklama: SwiGLU learns which feature channels pass through by multiplying one projection (xW_up) element-wise with the SiLU-activated version of the other (the gate). Clipping negatives to zero is the behavior of a ReLU FFN; since the FFN transforms each token independently, mixing across tokens belongs to attention.

sorular.soru: What is the key difference that distinguishes RoPE from classical absolute positional encoding?
secenekler: The position vector is added to the token embedding before the Transformer block; each slot receives its own vector.
Position information is added to the V vector; the attention output directly carries the token's absolute position.
Position is added to the pre-softmax scores as a learned bias that depends on the distance between tokens.
Q and K are rotated according to position; the Q·Kᵀ score depends on content match and the relative offset i−j.
sorular.aciklama: RoPE rotates the Q and K vectors according to position; the score (Rᵢqᵢ)·(Rⱼkⱼ) depends on both content match and the relative offset between i and j. The first option is classical absolute encoding of the form xᵢ = tokenᵢ + pᵢ; RoPE does not touch V and performs rotation rather than addition.

sorular.soru: Which statement about the relationship between GQA and KV cache is correct?
secenekler: GQA is an inference technique that replaces the KV cache; because past K/V are not stored at all, decode memory is reduced.
The KV cache can be applied only in models that use GQA or MQA; past K/V representations cannot be reused in MHA.
GQA takes effect only at inference; during training each Q head continues to use its own K/V head.
GQA is an architectural choice that reduces the number of cached K/V heads; the KV cache is a separate reuse mechanism.
sorular.aciklama: GQA changes the attention architecture, whereas KV caching separately reuses previous token representations. GQA is used in both training and inference; having 8 Q heads share 2 K/V pairs reduces the amount of K/V written to the cache by 4× but does not eliminate the cache. The KV cache also does not depend on GQA; it is used in MHA models as well.

sorular.soru: Which of the following correctly describes the mechanism that distinguishes MLA from GQA and MQA?
secenekler: It ties all Q heads to a single shared K/V head; Q diversity is preserved, and the cached representation is common.
It compresses the K/V state into a learned low-dimensional latent and caches that; K/V are recovered through projection.
It splits the Q heads into groups and ties each group to a small number of K/V heads; the number of cached heads drops to the number of groups.
It stores K/V values at a low bit width and rescales them at compute time; the head count and structure do not change.
sorular.aciklama: While GQA/MQA reduce the number of K/V heads through sharing, MLA reduces the token state to a compressed latent c via a down-projection; this compact latent is what is kept in the cache, and K/V-equivalent features are recovered through projection when needed. The first option is the definition of MQA and the third is that of GQA; MLA is more than merely a single shared KV head.

sorular.soru: In an MoE layer, the router scores are Expert 1: 0.72, Expert 2: 0.08, Expert 3: 0.15, Expert 4: 0.61, and top-2 routing is applied. How is the output produced for this token?
secenekler: Only Expert 1 and Expert 4 are run; their outputs are combined using the routing weights.
All four experts are run; only the outputs of the two experts with the highest scores are summed.
Only Expert 1 is run; Expert 4 is a backup expert that is activated when the router is undecided.
The outputs of all four experts are averaged; the scores are used only for load balancing during training.
sorular.aciklama: Top-2 routing selects the two experts with the highest scores (1 and 4); only these run, and their outputs are combined as a weighted sum using the routing weights, so computation per token stays sparse even though the total parameter count is large. Running all four experts would eliminate the 'sparse computation' advantage of MoE.

sorular.soru: Which pairing of model family and architectural features is correct?
secenekler: Mistral 7B — MLA-compressed KV latent and shared + routed MoE
LLaMA / Llama 2 — GQA and RMSNorm at all model sizes
DeepSeek V2/V3 — standard RoPE and a dense SwiGLU FFN
Mixtral 8×7B — GQA and an 8-expert MoE (Expert FFNs)
sorular.aciklama: Mixtral 8×7B uses RMSNorm, RoPE, GQA, and expert FFNs with 8 experts. In Llama 2, GQA is used only in the 70B model (the others use MHA); MLA and shared + routed MoE belong to DeepSeek V2/V3, and DeepSeek uses decoupled RoPE; Mistral 7B, meanwhile, is a dense model with GQA + sliding-window attention.

sorular.konu: Prefill vs. decode and KV cache
sorular.soru: Why is the decode phase generally memory-bandwidth-bound at small batch sizes, while prefill is compute-bound?
secenekler: Decode processes a single token, so there is little computation per byte of weights/KV read; prefill reuses the weights across many tokens.
In decode, the N × N attention score matrix is recomputed from scratch at every step; in prefill, the scores are computed once and stored in HBM.
In prefill, the weights are read from HBM separately for each token; in decode, the weights stay in on-chip SRAM and are not read.
In decode, softmax and sampling are executed on the CPU; in prefill, all matrix multiplications remain parallel on the GPU.
sorular.aciklama: Prefill processes many prompt tokens together, arithmetic intensity is high, and the weights are reused across tokens; in decode, all weights and the KV cache are read for a single token, so memory reads become the dominant cost. Thanks to the KV cache, decode does not recompute the N × N scores from scratch, which is why the second option is wrong.

sorular.konu: Prefill vs. decode and KV cache
sorular.soru: The prompt has 5 tokens and the model generates 4 tokens. Counting the positions processed, how many positions are processed in total without the KV cache and with the KV cache?
secenekler: 26 and 8
35 and 9
26 and 4
20 and 4
sorular.aciklama: Generating 4 tokens requires 4 forward passes: prefill processes 5 positions, then the decode steps without a cache process 6, 7, and 8 positions (total 26); with the cache, prefill 5 + only the newest token at each decode step (1+1+1) = 8. There is no extra pass that processes the last generated token; '35 and 9' counts this extra step. The cached count also includes the 5 prefill positions, which is why '26 and 4' is wrong.

sorular.konu: Prefill vs. decode and KV cache
sorular.soru: Consider a GQA model with 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, and BF16, which needs 128 KiB of KV cache per token and 512 MiB for 4,096 tokens. If the same model used MHA with 32 KV heads instead of GQA, approximately how large would the KV cache be for a single 4,096-token request?
secenekler: 512 MiB
1 GiB
2 GiB
8 GiB
sorular.aciklama: In the formula 2 (K,V) × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes, raising the KV head count from 8 to 32 increases the per-token cost by 4×: 512 KiB/token × 4,096 ≈ 2 GiB. 8 GiB is the value obtained by additionally multiplying by 4 concurrent requests; 512 MiB assumes the number of KV heads does not affect the cache size.

sorular.soru: Which of the following statements about FlashAttention is false?
secenekler: It normalizes the softmax of each Q/K tile independently and then sums the tile outputs.
It produces the same mathematical result as standard attention; the gain comes from memory traffic.
It avoids writing the entire N × N intermediate score matrix to HBM and reading it back.
It updates running softmax statistics while processing small tiles on-chip.
sorular.aciklama: Tiles share running softmax statistics and each tile is not normalized independently; otherwise the result would deviate from standard attention. The other three statements are accurate: the same math, the N × N matrix not being written to HBM, and the online softmax update.

sorular.soru: A GPU has 24 physical KV blocks. Requests A, B, and C use 2, 4, and 6 blocks respectively; a fixed-reservation scheme allocates 8 blocks to each request. In which scheme does a new request D that needs 3 blocks find space immediately?
secenekler: In both schemes; in each, 12 blocks are in use and 12 blocks are free.
Only in paged allocation; in fixed reservation, all 24 blocks are already allocated.
Only in fixed reservation; in paged allocation, the blocks are scattered, so 3 contiguous blocks cannot be found.
In neither; adding 3 more blocks to the 12 used blocks exceeds the capacity limit.
sorular.aciklama: In fixed reservation, 3 × 8 = 24 blocks are allocated; even though 12 of them sit unused, they are 'reserved but idle' and cannot be given to D. Paged allocation occupies only the 12 blocks actually in use, 12 blocks are genuinely free, and blocks need not be physically contiguous (the block table maps logical blocks to scattered pages); therefore the reasoning of the third option is invalid.

sorular.soru: Suppose request A finishes at t2 and request C finishes at t3. What exactly is the difference that continuous batching provides compared with static batching?
secenekler: Because more requests are processed at each step, the decode step of a single request becomes shorter.
All requests complete in the same step, so the KV cache is released all at once.
Long prompts are split into chunks and interleaved between B's decode steps.
Requests D and E are admitted into the freed slots; the slots do not sit idle until B finishes.
sorular.aciklama: In static batching, the group stays the same until the longest request in the batch (B) finishes, and the slots of A and C sit idle; in continuous batching, the vLLM scheduler reselects the active requests at every decode step and admits D or E into a freed slot. The third option describes chunked prefill, not continuous batching itself.

sorular.soru: Measurements on a serving system show high TTFT but low ITL/TPOT. According to the principle 'measure first, then choose the optimization', which conclusion is correct?
secenekler: The latency is in the decode steps; per-step cost should be reduced with speculative decoding.
The latency is in queuing or the prefill phase; techniques that speed up decode do not fix TTFT.
The bottleneck is throughput; reducing the batch size makes the first token be produced earlier.
The bottleneck is KV cache reads; quantizing the KV to INT8 shortens the time to first token.
sorular.aciklama: TTFT measures the start (queue + prefill), whereas ITL/TPOT measure token generation speed; if ITL is low, decode is already fast, and decode-focused techniques such as speculative decoding do not speed up the first token. KV cache reads are costly during the decode step and are not the determinant of TTFT.

sorular.soru: Using symmetric integer quantization (q = round(w / s), ŵ = q × s), the weight w = 0.736 is quantized with scale s = 0.05. What are the stored integer q and the reconstructed ŵ?
sorular.aciklama: 0.736 / 0.05 = 14.72 → rounding gives q = 15; ŵ = 15 × 0.05 = 0.75 (reconstruction error +0.014). q = 14 is a round-down error; ŵ is always q × s, so the original 0.736 is not recovered; q = 74 would result from a scale of s = 0.01.

sorular.soru: In speculative decoding, the draft model proposes 'on, the, mat'; the target accepts 'on' and 'the' and picks 'sofa' instead of 'mat'. For these three output tokens, how many sequential forward passes does the large target model make, compared with standard decode?
secenekler: 1 vs. 3: a single verification pass scores all positions and picks 'sofa' at the first mismatch.
2 vs. 3: one verification pass, followed by a separate correction pass for 'sofa'.
3 vs. 3: the target still computes each position one by one; the gain comes only from the draft being cheap.
4 vs. 3: the three draft passes are added to the target cost, so the total number of passes increases.
sorular.aciklama: Standard decode requires three sequential target passes; in speculative decoding, the target scores all draft positions in a single verification pass, accepts the matching ones, and supplies its own choice ('sofa') at the first mismatch, so no separate correction pass is needed. The draft passes belong to the small model and are not counted toward the target cost; the speedup depends on the acceptance rate and the verification cost.

sorular.soru: A team will serve many requests that all begin with the same long agent instruction. Which engine and mechanism focus on this workload?
secenekler: Ollama — loads the model locally and answers a single user's request on a laptop.
vLLM — batches active requests and allocates GPU KV pages per request.
SGLang — detects the matching prefix and reuses the cached K/V.
vLLM — combines MLA and MoE in a single model as a new LLM architecture.
sorular.aciklama: SGLang is paired with the 'reused context' scenario: the prefix of the shared long instruction is detected, the K/V is reused, and only the unique part is generated. vLLM focuses on batching many concurrent requests and, is a serving engine rather than a new LLM; Ollama is for single-user local use.
